```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(width = 110)
library(sciparseR)
ex <- function(f) system.file("extdata", f, package = "sciparseR")
```

Published papers contain errors, and extraction adds its own. The
fixture `contradictory.pdf` plants five problems: a hazard ratio that
differs between text (0.62) and table (0.68), 130 events among 120
patients, an odds ratio of 1.8 with a confidence interval of 2.1 to 3.0,
a p-value of 1.30, and a table confidence interval (0.45 to 1.02) that
includes 1 next to p = 0.02.

```{r}
doc <- sc_parse(ex("contradictory.pdf"))
x <- sc_validate(sc_extract(doc, "clinical_trial"))
x
```

## The rules

```{r}
v <- x$validation
v[v$result != "pass", c("rule", "severity", "result", "message")]
```

| Rule | Checks |
|---|---|
| `count_nonnegative` | counts are non-negative integers, denominators positive |
| `events_le_denominator` | events do not exceed the denominator |
| `percent_consistent` | a percentage matches events / denominator within its rounding |
| `ci_ordered` | lower < upper, estimate inside |
| `ratio_positive` | ratio estimates and limits are positive |
| `p_range` | 0 &le; p &le; 1 |
| `p_ci_agreement` | a 95% CI excludes the null exactly when p < 0.05 |
| `estimate_bound` | an estimate names its outcome and both arms |
| `dispersion_type` | a dispersion is labelled SD or SE |
| `analyzed_le_randomized` | analyzed &le; randomized |
| `arm_sizes_sum` | per arm allocations add up to the randomized number |
| `timepoint_bound` | values without a time point when the outcome has several |
| `cross_source_conflict` | text and table agree on the same quantity |
| `type` | numeric fields parse as numbers |

The conflict rule compares two values only when outcome, measure and
statistic match. If arms, time point, analysis set or adjustment differ,
they are not compared. If one side leaves them unbound (a sentence such as
"the hazard ratio for death was 0.57" names no arms and no time point), a
difference is a `possible_conflict`, not a certain one.

Each record gets the worst result of the rules that touched it:

```{r}
table(x$records$validation_status, useNA = "ifany")
```

A reported value that fails an error rule gets the status
`inconsistent`. It stays in the records and in the review queue, but
`sc_derive()` never uses it as an input:

```{r}
x$records[x$records$status == "inconsistent", c("field", "statistic", "value", "outcome")]
```

## The review queue

```{r}
q <- sc_review_queue(x)
q[, c("priority", "field", "statistic", "value", "outcome", "reason")]
```

Priority 1 is errors and unverifiable values, 2 warnings, 3 statuses such
as `missing` or `not_reported` that a reviewer should confirm.

## Exceptions

Some findings are real features of the paper, not errors to fix. They can
be accepted with a written justification, and stay visible as
`exception`:

```{r}
obs <- v$observation_id[v$rule == "p_range" & v$result == "fail"]
ex_tab <- data.frame(rule = "p_range", id = obs,
                     justification = "P = 1.30 is printed in the source; reported to the journal")
v2 <- sc_validate(x, exceptions = ex_tab)$validation
v2[v2$rule == "p_range", c("result", "justification")]
```

## Corrections

A reviewer's correction is a new record. The original stays, marked
`superseded`, and the new record names the reviewer, the reason and the
record it replaces. Its evidence is the original's evidence.

```{r}
t2 <- sc_extract(sc_parse(ex("trial_tables.pdf")), "numerical_results")
id <- t2$records$record_id[which(t2$records$statistic == "dispersion")][1]
t2 <- sc_correct(t2, id, value = "13.2", reviewer = "reviewer 1",
                 reason = "Statistical methods state values are mean and SD",
                 statistic = "sd", dispersion_type = "sd")
t2$records[t2$records$record_id == id | t2$records$supersedes %in% id,
           c("record_id", "statistic", "value", "status", "data_origin", "supersedes", "reviewer")]
```

## Derived values

Meta-analysis often needs values that the paper does not print, such as
the standard error of a log hazard ratio. `sc_derive()` computes them as
separate records with `data_origin = "derived"`, the ids of their inputs,
the formula and the software:

```{r}
d <- sc_derive(sc_extract(sc_parse(ex("trial_tables.pdf"))), c("log_ratio", "se_log_ratio"))
dv <- d$records[d$records$data_origin == "derived", ]
dv[, c("outcome", "arm", "statistic", "value", "inputs", "formula")]
```

An SD from an SE needs the number of patients *analyzed* for that result.
sciparseR uses an n reported with the result, or one you supply. The
allocated arm size is used only when you ask for it, and the record then
says that it is an assumption, because the number analyzed is often
smaller than the number randomized:

```{r}
e <- sc_extract(sc_parse(ex("trial_tables.pdf")))
nrow(sc_derive(e, "sd_from_se")$records) == nrow(e$records)
s1 <- sc_derive(e, "sd_from_se", n = c("Drug A" = 118, "placebo" = 117))$records
s1[s1$statistic %in% "sd", c("arm", "value", "notes")]
s2 <- sc_derive(e, "sd_from_se", allow_randomized_n = TRUE)$records
s2$notes[s2$statistic %in% "sd"][1]
```

Derivations never guess a missing input. A confidence interval without a
stated level is skipped unless you set `assume_level`, and the assumption
is written into the record:

```{r}
u <- sc_extract(sc_parse(ex("trial_tables.pdf")))
u$records$ci_level <- NA_real_
nrow(sc_derive(u, "se_log_ratio")$records) == nrow(u$records)
a <- sc_derive(u, "se_log_ratio", assume_level = 95)$records
unique(a$notes[a$statistic %in% "se_log"])
```

Derived records are excluded from validation: they are checked through
their inputs.
